{{< include ../_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

tidymodels, glmnet, and xgboost are too large to run in a browser, so these exercises practise the ideas of Chapter 12 with functions that come with R: prediction errors, overfitting with `lm()`, and boosting built by hand from small rpart trees. The downloadable project at the bottom uses tidymodels, exactly as in the chapter. Where you see `______`, replace it with your own code.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [ex1, ex2, ex3, ex4, ex5, ex6]
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(rpart)
students      <- read.csv("students.csv")
semesters     <- read.csv("semesters.csv")
questionnaire <- read.csv("questionnaire.csv")

year_one <- semesters |>
  filter(semester <= 2) |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = student_id, names_from = semester,
              values_from = gpa:wellbeing, names_glue = "{.value}_s{semester}")
final_gpa <- semesters |>
  filter(semester == 4, !is.na(gpa)) |>
  select(student_id, final_gpa = gpa)
gpa_data <- students |>
  select(student_id, age, financial_worry) |>
  left_join(questionnaire, join_by(student_id)) |>
  left_join(year_one, join_by(student_id)) |>
  inner_join(final_gpa, join_by(student_id)) |>
  select(-student_id) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) replace(x, is.na(x), median(x, na.rm = TRUE))))

set.seed(12)
train_rows <- sample(nrow(gpa_data), round(0.75 * nrow(gpa_data)))
train <- gpa_data[train_rows, ]
test  <- gpa_data[-train_rows, ]

rmse <- function(actual, predicted) sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))

tiny <- data.frame(
  actual    = c(3.2, 2.8, 3.6, 3.0, 2.5),
  predicted = c(3.0, 2.9, 3.3, 3.1, 2.9)
)
```

## Measuring prediction error

### Exercise 1: MAE and RMSE by hand

The setup code has created the chapter's five students, `tiny`, with actual and predicted final GPAs. Calculate the errors, then the MAE (the mean of the absolute errors) and the RMSE (the square root of the mean of the squared errors).

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1
errors <- tiny$actual - tiny$predicted
mean(abs(______))        # MAE
sqrt(mean(______^2))     # RMSE
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
errors <- tiny$actual - tiny$predicted
mean(abs(errors))
sqrt(mean(errors^2))
```

The MAE is 0.22 and the RMSE 0.25. Now change the last prediction to 3.5, so that it is off by 1.0 (`tiny$predicted[5] <- 3.5`) and run both again: the MAE rises to 0.34 but the RMSE to 0.48, because squaring gives the big miss much more weight.
:::
:::

### Exercise 2: The baseline

The simplest prediction gives every test student the average final GPA of the *training* students. What is its RMSE on the test set? (`rmse()` is defined in the setup.)

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2
baseline <- mean(train$______)
rmse(test$final_gpa, ______)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex2" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
baseline <- mean(train$final_gpa)
rmse(test$final_gpa, baseline)
```

About 0.32. Every useful model must do clearly better than this.
:::
:::

## Too many predictors

### Exercise 3: Overfitting with a small sample

`gpa_data` has 38 predictors (the questionnaire items, age, financial worry, and the year-one records; missing values have been filled in with medians). Fit a regression with all of them (`final_gpa ~ .`) on just 60 training students, and compare its RMSE on those 60 students with its RMSE on the test set.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3
set.seed(3)
small <- train[sample(nrow(train), 60), ]
big_model <- lm(final_gpa ~ ., data = small)
rmse(small$final_gpa, predict(big_model, small))   # on its own students
rmse(test$final_gpa, predict(big_model, ______))   # on new students
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
rmse(small$final_gpa, predict(big_model, small))
rmse(test$final_gpa, predict(big_model, test))
```

On its own 60 students the model looks excellent (an RMSE of about 0.12), but on new students its RMSE is about 0.32, hardly better than the baseline of Exercise 2. With 38 coefficients estimated from 60 students, the model has fitted the noise in its sample.
:::
:::

### Exercise 4: Fewer predictors

Now fit a regression on the same 60 students with only the two year-one GPAs, `gpa_s1` and `gpa_s2`. How does it do on new students?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4
set.seed(3)
small <- train[sample(nrow(train), 60), ]
small_model <- lm(final_gpa ~ ______ + ______, data = small)
rmse(test$final_gpa, predict(small_model, test))
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex4" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
small_model <- lm(final_gpa ~ gpa_s1 + gpa_s2, data = small)
rmse(test$final_gpa, predict(small_model, test))
```

About 0.2: far better than the model with every predictor. Choosing the predictors by hand works here because we know that past grades matter most. The lasso of the chapter makes this choice automatically, from the data.
:::
:::

## Boosting by hand

### Exercise 5: Two rounds of boosting

Boosting starts with the average, then fits a small tree to the errors, adds a fraction of its predictions (the learning rate), and repeats. Complete the second round, and see how the training RMSE falls.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5
learn_rate <- 0.3
prediction <- rep(mean(train$final_gpa), nrow(train))   # start: the average
rmse(train$final_gpa, prediction)

# Round 1: a one-split tree fitted to the errors
train$error <- train$final_gpa - prediction
tree1 <- rpart(error ~ . - final_gpa, data = train, control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 1))
prediction <- prediction + learn_rate * predict(tree1, train)
rmse(train$final_gpa, prediction)

# Round 2: the same, fitted to the new errors
train$error <- train$final_gpa - ______
tree2 <- rpart(error ~ . - final_gpa, data = train, control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 1))
prediction <- prediction + learn_rate * predict(______, train)
rmse(train$final_gpa, prediction)
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Round 2 repeats round 1 exactly, using the updated `prediction` and the new tree, `tree2`. `. - final_gpa` means "every column except `final_gpa`", so the tree cannot peek at the answer.
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
train$error <- train$final_gpa - prediction
tree2 <- rpart(error ~ . - final_gpa, data = train, control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 1))
prediction <- prediction + learn_rate * predict(tree2, train)
rmse(train$final_gpa, prediction)
```

Each round lowers the RMSE a little. Each tree asks one question (print `tree1` and `tree2` to see which), and the model improves in small steps.
:::
:::

### Exercise 6: Many rounds

Put the rounds in a loop: 100 rounds, keeping track of the test RMSE. How low does it get, and how does that compare with the baseline (Exercise 2)?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6
learn_rate <- 0.3
n_rounds <- ______
pred_train <- rep(mean(train$final_gpa), nrow(train))
pred_test  <- rep(mean(train$final_gpa), nrow(test))
test_rmse <- numeric(n_rounds)
for (i in 1:n_rounds) {
  train$error <- train$final_gpa - pred_train
  tree <- rpart(error ~ . - final_gpa, data = train, control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 1))
  pred_train <- pred_train + learn_rate * predict(tree, train)
  pred_test  <- pred_test  + learn_rate * predict(tree, test)
  test_rmse[i] <- rmse(test$final_gpa, pred_test)
}
plot(test_rmse, type = "l", xlab = "Number of trees", ylab = "Test RMSE")
min(test_rmse)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex6" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
n_rounds <- 100
```

The test RMSE falls quickly over the first 20 or so trees, then levels off at about 0.2, far below the baseline of about 0.32. This is boosting: XGBoost does the same, only much faster and with extra refinements.
:::
:::
